idiom_name: pure object functions over immutable case classes returning Either
implementation_notes: The core is a set of pure `object` functions over immutable `case class` values returning `Either[Problem, Result]`; nothing in it touches a driver, `java.time.Clock`, `scala.io` or a `Future`. The shell is `main` or the HTTP route: it loads the data, calls the core and folds the `Either` into a response. `case class`/`val` replaces the classic immutable Value Object, and passing the data (instead of an injected service) replaces the port: where a decision needs something from outside, that something is a parameter. Keep the DI service shape only where a framework constructs it; it buys nothing for pure decisions.
pitfalls: `case class` is shallowly immutable: a `List`/`Map` field still exposes the collection (and `copy()` shares the same instances), so pass immutable collections and avoid holding mutable builders in the core.
`Future` is an effect: a core method returning `Future` starts work on an `ExecutionContext` when called and drags `Await`/timeouts into tests; keep the core's return types effect-free.
Throwing inside the core (or `Either.cond` with a side-effecting predicate) hides the effect and forces the shell into `Try`; use `Left`/`Right` and convert once at the boundary.

variants.name: cats-effect IO + IOApp shell
variants.idiom_name: IO values as descriptions; IOApp.run as the imperative shell
variants.implementation_notes: cats-effect turns effects into values: `IO[A]` is a pure, lazy description, so the application is composed as `IO` values and `IOApp.run` is the shell that finally executes them, wiring resources with `Resource`/`bracket` and returning an `ExitCode`. Decisions stay plain functions that the `IO` pipeline maps over, which keeps them testable without the runtime; `IOApp` installs interruption handling, so shutdown and cancellation land in the shell where they belong. Choose it when the application is already effect-based - for a pure decision module it adds a runtime and type-class vocabulary you do not need.
pitfalls: `IO` values are lazy: a pure decision placed in a strict `val` runs when the object is constructed, not when the pipeline executes - keep decisions as `def`s or plain arguments.
Letting `IO` into the core's signatures forces every caller into the effect type; the point of the pattern is that the decisions are not effectful, so only the shell should be `IO`-shaped.
Resource leaks are silent in `IO` unless acquisition uses `Resource`/`bracket`, and `unsafeRunSync` inside the core is a reliable sign the core was written as effects rather than as values.
